items.title: Grief circle
items.body: Eight weeks, rolling. Hand work only, because scissors and grief need supervision and conversation.

items.title: Hospital kits
items.body: Assembled by volunteers, distributed through the cancer center and two dialysis units.

items.title: Re-entry circle
items.body: Wednesday afternoons with a paid instructor, machines provided, materials to keep.

items.title: Family memory mornings
items.body: One Saturday a month, by appointment, with as much silence as a family needs.

sections.heading: Who the circles are for
sections.html: Anyone. No diagnosis, referral, or paperwork is required, and no experience is expected; half the stitches learned here are the first ones. Everything made in a circle belongs to the maker, and nothing made here is graded, judged, or photographed without permission.

items.q: Do I need to know how to sew?
items.a: No. The circles teach the stitch being used that evening, and unfinished is a word we do not use here.
No. Materials, instruction, and childcare during circles are covered by Friends of the collective.
Once, sometimes, is exactly right. The chair will be there the following week if you want it again.

sections.title: Support the work
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: Friends memberships, fabric donations, and the specific magic of twelve dollars.

sections.heading: Where the money goes
sections.html: Twelve dollars assembles one hospital kit. Forty stocks a circle's materials for a month. A hundred keeps the childcare room open on a Tuesday. The ledger is read at the annual potluck and posted to the members' area, because trust is part of the care.

sections.title: Become a Friend
sections.body: Friends receive the quarterly letter and the satisfaction of a shelf that stays stocked.

sections.title: About the collective
sections.subtitle: Sample text — replace me: Founded in a hospice hallway with two quilting frames and a social worker who could thread a needle in the dark.

sections.html:
The first circle formed around a family who could not sit still in the waiting room and a volunteer who could not watch them try. She brought in a quilting frame, and the hallway filled with people who had something to do with their hands while they waited. The hospice asked her back. The program outgrew the hallway in a year.

The collective now runs four programs on donations and stubbornness, with one part-time coordinator, a rotating cast of volunteers, and a firm rule that care stays free at the door.

items.quote: In twenty years of practice I have prescribed a lot of things. This is the only one patients thank me for with their hands busy.
items.author: An oncology social worker

sections.heading: What we can accept
sections.html: Soft washed cotton, flannel, and perle cotton thread are always in season. We cannot accept batting scraps or polyester for the hospital kits, and the donation door answer is on the answering machine, which is staffed by a volunteer with strong opinions.
